specPoints.text: understand how to classify a substance as an element, compound or mixture

primer.text: You already know from States of Matter that every substance is built from particles. This note uses that idea to sort every substance into one of three families — an element, a compound or a mixture — by asking two questions: are the atoms all of the same kind, and are any different kinds chemically joined?

lessons.title: Elements and Compounds
lessons.opening: Every substance in chemistry belongs to exactly one of three families: an element, a compound or a mixture. This lesson takes the two families whose particles are chemically joined — elements, where every atom holds the same number of protons, and compounds, where two or more different elements are bonded into something new that behaves as one substance.
keyPoints: All substances fall into exactly one of three classes: element, compound or mixture.
An element is made of atoms that all hold the same number of protons.
The periodic table holds 118 elements, for example copper, iron and magnesium.
A compound joins two or more different elements by chemical bonds into one substance.
No physical method can split a compound back into the elements it contains.

low.restatement: Everything is either an element (one kind of atom), a compound (different atoms bonded) or a mixture (things merely placed together). Elements cannot be broken into anything simpler; compounds cannot be undone by physical means.
low.analogy: Think of building bricks: an element is one brick type, a compound is bricks glued into a fixed model, and a mixture is a drawer of loose and glued pieces shaken together.
low.examPointer: Quote both halves of the element definition: one proton count throughout, and nothing simpler can be got out of it.

medium.restatement: An element keeps one proton count in every atom, so no chemical or physical process can free anything simpler from it. A compound is different elements reacted together into one substance whose parts cannot be pulled apart by filtering, magnetising or evaporating.
medium.analogy: A compound is like a cake: eggs and flour have reacted into something new, and no sieve will hand you the eggs back. A mixture is still the separate ingredients sitting in one bowl.
medium.examPointer: Classification questions usually turn on one phrase — chemically combined. Write it for compounds, and withhold it for mixtures.

check.stem: What makes all the atoms of one element identical to each other?

options.text: They all contain the same number of protons
options.explanation: One proton count across every atom is the defining feature of an element.

options.text: They all have the same mass
options.explanation: Neutron numbers can differ between atoms of the same element, so mass is not the marker.

options.text: They all look the same under a microscope
options.explanation: Appearance is not the chemical criterion; atoms of one element share a proton count, not looks.

options.text: They all refuse to bond with anything
options.explanation: Elements do react and bond; the definition concerns proton count, not reactivity.

check.stem: A student claims that because copper cannot be split into anything simpler, copper can never change at all. What is the flaw?

options.text: Cannot be split refers to separating it into simpler substances, not to chemical change
options.explanation: Copper stays an element only while unbonded; it readily takes part in reactions that build compounds.

options.text: Copper is actually a compound, so the claim fails twice
options.explanation: Copper holds one proton count throughout, which is exactly what an element is.

options.text: Splitting and reacting are the same process described in two words
options.explanation: Splitting means separating into simpler parts; reacting means bonding to build new substances.

options.text: Copper can be split if heated gently enough
options.explanation: No physical method, gentle or harsh, divides an element into simpler substances.

check.stem: Carbon dioxide contains carbon and oxygen. Why is it a compound rather than a mixture?

options.text: The two elements are chemically combined into one fixed substance
options.explanation: Chemical bonds join the carbon to the oxygen, which is precisely the compound criterion.

options.text: It contains two different substances floating loosely together
options.explanation: The carbon and oxygen are bonded into one substance, not floating separately.

options.text: It is made of molecules, and every molecule is a compound
options.explanation: An oxygen molecule pairs two identical atoms and stays an element, so molecule does not imply compound.

options.text: Because it is a gas at room temperature
options.explanation: State of matter has no bearing on class; gases can be elements, compounds or mixtures.

check.stem: Which line classifies copper(II) sulfate, CuSO4, correctly?

options.text: A compound, because three elements are chemically combined within it
options.explanation: Copper, sulfur and oxygen are bonded into one substance, which is the compound definition at work.

options.text: An element, because the name begins with copper
options.explanation: The name borrows from copper, but the substance holds three elements bonded together.

options.text: A mixture, because it contains several substances
options.explanation: It is one bonded substance, not several substances placed side by side.

options.text: None of the three, because salts sit outside the classes
options.explanation: The three classes cover every substance; a pure salt sits inside the compound class.

check.stem: A poster sorts substances into four boxes: element, compound, mixture and other. What is wrong with the fourth box?

options.text: It is unnecessary, because the first three already cover every substance
options.explanation: The three-way sort is exhaustive, so the fourth box stays empty forever.

options.text: Some substances are part element and part compound by nature
options.explanation: A substance is one or the other; hybrid classes do not exist in this scheme.

options.text: The boxes apply only to pure samples prepared in a laboratory
options.explanation: Every substance anywhere — sand, air, milk — falls into one of the three classes.

options.text: The fourth box is needed for elements not yet discovered
options.explanation: Any future substance will still be an element, a compound or a mixture.

lessons.title: Mixtures and Classification
sourceHeadings: Particle diagram showing elements, compounds and mixtures
lessons.opening: A mixture is what you get when two or more substances — elements, compounds or both — share a space without chemically joining. Because no bonds form, ordinary physical methods such as filtration or evaporation can pull the ingredients apart again, and particle diagrams make the contrast visible: bonded units of one kind signal a compound, while several different units loose in the same frame signal a mixture.
keyPoints: A mixture holds two or more substances in one place without chemical bonds between them.
The ingredients of a mixture can be elements, compounds or both at once.
Physical methods such as filtration or evaporation separate mixtures into their parts.
Sand in water, oil in water and sulfur mixed with iron filings are all mixtures.
In particle diagrams, a mixture shows different atoms or molecules sharing the space unbonded.

low.restatement: A mixture is substances sitting together, not bonded together. Because the ingredients keep their separate identities, filtering, evaporating or other physical tricks recover each one unchanged.
low.analogy: It is a bowl of mixed nuts: almonds and cashews share the bowl, stay themselves, and you can pick them apart by hand.
low.examPointer: The examiner rewards the phrase chemically combined — attach it to compounds, and withhold it from mixtures.

medium.restatement: Two or more substances count as a mixture whenever no chemical bonds link them, so each keeps its own melting point, appearance and behaviour. Filtration or evaporation then works, because separating a mixture breaks no bond at all.
medium.analogy: Breakfast cereal with nuts and raisins is a mixture: every piece keeps its crunch, and picking the raisins out costs patience, not chemistry.
medium.examPointer: For diagram questions, count the atom types first: one kind means element, one bonded kind means compound, several kinds together means mixture.

check.stem: Stirring sand into water gives cloudy water. How is the result classified, and why?

options.text: A mixture — the sand and the water are not chemically combined
options.explanation: Two substances sharing a space with no bonds between them form a mixture.

options.text: A compound — two substances have combined into one
options.explanation: Combining without chemical bonds is mixing, not compound formation.

options.text: An element — only one kind of liquid is visible
options.explanation: Visibility decides nothing about class; two substances are present even if one is hidden from view.

options.text: A compound, because the sand dissolves into the water
options.explanation: The sand does not dissolve here; and even dissolving leaves a mixture, never a compound.

check.stem: Why can filtration or evaporation separate the ingredients of a mixture but never the elements inside a compound?

options.text: Mixtures hold no chemical bonds to break, so physical methods suffice
options.explanation: Physical methods cannot break chemical bonds, which is why compounds resist every one of them.

options.text: Physical methods are simply too weak to disturb a compound
options.explanation: Strength is not the issue; no physical process targets the bonds inside a compound.

options.text: Compounds separate when heated to a high enough temperature
options.explanation: Decomposition by heat is a chemical change, not a physical separation.

options.text: Filtration works on compounds provided the filter paper is fine enough
options.explanation: Filter fineness cannot undo chemical combination.

check.stem: A particle diagram shows three separate two-atom units, each bonding one black sphere to one white sphere, and nothing else. What is shown?

options.text: A compound — one kind of chemically combined atom pair, repeated
options.explanation: Identical bonded pairs of two different atoms depict a single compound.

options.text: A mixture of two elements
options.explanation: The spheres are bonded in pairs, not loose, and each pair holds two different atoms.

options.text: An element, because every unit looks the same
options.explanation: Sameness of unit with two different atom types is the compound signature.

options.text: A mixture of two compounds
options.explanation: Only one kind of unit is present, so nothing is mixed.

check.stem: Oil floated on water is shaken and then settles back into two layers. Classify the result and justify it.

options.text: A mixture — two substances in contact with no chemical combination
options.explanation: Layering changes nothing; the oil and the water remain separate substances.

options.text: A compound — the shaking made them combine
options.explanation: Shaking mixes; it does not bond, and the layers returning is itself evidence of no bonding.

options.text: A compound, because the boundary between the layers is sharp
options.explanation: A sharp boundary shows the substances refused to combine — the mark of a mixture.

options.text: An element, because water is present
options.explanation: Water is itself a compound, and its presence alongside oil makes the whole a mixture.

check.stem: The exam hands you an unfamiliar substance described only in words and asks which of the three classes it belongs to. What habit earns the marks?

options.text: Ask two questions: are all atoms the same kind, and are different atoms chemically joined
options.explanation: Same atoms means element; different atoms bonded means compound; different substances unbonded means mixture.

options.text: Name its state of matter first, since class depends on it
options.explanation: Solid, liquid or gas, the three classes apply equally; state is irrelevant.

options.text: Guess element whenever the sample has a single colour
options.explanation: Colour carries no class information at all.

options.text: Call any white powder a mixture to be safe
options.explanation: Classification is decided by structure, not hedging; many white powders are pure compounds.

glossary.definition: A substance whose atoms all hold the same number of protons and that cannot be split into anything simpler.
A pure substance made of two or more different elements chemically combined.
The chart of all 118 elements, on which every element has its place.
Two or more substances sharing a space without chemical bonds between them.
A physical method that separates an insoluble solid from a liquid by passing the mixture through paper.
A physical method that separates a dissolved solid from its liquid by turning the liquid to gas.
A drawing that uses spheres to show the atoms or molecules present in a sample.

workedExample.prompt: Classify each substance as an element, a compound or a mixture, and justify each answer: a) copper, Cu; b) copper(II) sulfate, CuSO4; c) iron filings stirred together with sulfur powder.
steps: a) Copper is an element: all of its atoms hold the same number of protons, and it cannot be split into anything simpler.
b) Copper(II) sulfate is a compound: two or more different elements are chemically combined, and no physical method separates it back into copper, sulfur and oxygen.
c) Iron filings mixed with sulfur powder form a mixture: the substances share the space without chemical bonds between them.
Because no bonds form in a mixture, a physical method such as using a magnet would recover the iron unchanged — compounds never separate this way.
workedExample.finalAnswer: a) Element. b) Compound (different elements chemically combined). c) Mixture (no chemical bonds; separable by physical means).
